水琴窟不採持琴方式演奏。基本操作是站在手水鉢前，讓水從壺頂部約兩公分洞口滴入或潑: The suikinkutsu is not played by holding an instrument. The basic action is to stand at the water basin and let water drip or be splashed through the hole about two centimetres wide at the top of the jar into the small pool inside; with a single-jar installation the sound often comes of itself as you rinse your hands, while a two-jar one means deliberately splashing water toward two particular openings. As it sounds, the first drips make a running-water note and the later drips a dripping note; if there is a bamboo tube nearby, set one end on the ground near the mouth of the jar and put the other to your ear to amplify the sound. For a beginner the point is to control the amount of water and where it falls, so that the water really enters the hole instead of merely running over the basin.
水琴窟具有清澈透亮的音色，帶有明快而靈動的質感。其音域集中於中高音區，宛如風鈴或: The suikinkutsu has a clear, limpid timbre with a bright, nimble quality. Its range is concentrated in the middle and upper register, limpid as a wind chime or a drop of water. When water drips into the clay jar the enclosed space resonates, giving the sound a natural echo and depth and many layers. Its colour combines the crispness of metal instruments with the warmth of wooden ones, like the attack of a glockenspiel or a marimba but softer and more flowing. The sound swells and fades of itself and carries a Zen stillness: it keeps the instrument's own identity while holding the soothing quality particular to water, and it creates an image of quiet that reaches far.
水琴窟的發聲主體為倒埋地下的壺，早期多用儲存米或水的陶壺，有釉與無釉皆可，未上釉: The sounding body of the suikinkutsu is a jar buried upside down in the ground; early ones were mostly clay jars used for storing rice or water, glazed or unglazed, and unglazed jars are thought better because their rougher surface forms drips more easily; metal ones have also appeared recently. The jar is about thirty centimetres to one metre high and thirty to fifty centimetres across, with an opening about two centimetres wide at the top. It usually stands on gravel, with a seal of earth or clay at the bottom to hold the water, and a drain pipe to control the water level; pottery tiles may be used at the sides, and fist-sized stones cover the top. Some installations add a bamboo tube, one end on the ground near the top of the jar and the other at the ear, to amplify the sound.
水琴窟舊稱洞水門，最初作為洗手池旁倒埋的排水器，因排水聲而被園丁調整發聲。江戶中: The suikinkutsu was formerly called dōsuimon and began as a drain buried beside a hand-washing basin, whose draining sound gardeners then tuned into music. It became popular in the middle Edo period (1603–1867) along with the development of the water basin, and the garden of Kobori Enshū had one; he is often taken to be its inventor. Production declined at the end of the Edo period and it became popular again in the Meiji period (1867–1912). By the early twentieth century it was almost forgotten, and in 1959 Hirayama Katsuzō of Tokyo University of Agriculture reported only two, both out of repair. In 1982 the Asahi Shimbun carried a report soliciting information, and in 1985 a Nippon Television programme sparked a revival; new installations increased, and modern types appeared in metal, indoors, with amplification and with sound carried through tubes.
水琴窟（日語：水琴窟／すいきんくつ，羅馬化：Suikinkutsu）是指一種日本: The suikinkutsu (Japanese: 水琴窟 / すいきんくつ, romanised: Suikinkutsu) is a Japanese garden ornament and instrument. It consists of an inverted, sealed jar: water runs through a hole in the upper part and falls into a small pool inside, making a pleasing sound of water striking water that resembles a bell or a Japanese koto. A suikinkutsu is usually set beside a water basin, and such basins often stand at the entrance to a tea room, for guests at a tea ceremony to rinse their hands.
